title: The flood peaked
description: Linux 7.4-rc2 carries a small miracle: in eBPF, fixes are landing faster than AI-generated bug reports. The flood didn't end. The job moved — from finding to judging, and judgment is still ours.

title: Read-only is a promise, not a property
description: Claude can now read two years of your bank transactions through Plaid — read-only, no ads, no moving money. Read-only sounds like a property of the system. It is a promise, and promises get renegotiated.

title: Your AI dreams about you now
description: Anthropic's Claude dreams between sessions: rereading its logs, correcting wrong notes, building wikis. The model that remembered nine things beat the one that remembered 413. Memory isn't a recording. It's a point of view — and you're not the author.

title: 44% of the science expired
description: Stanford retested fifty famous findings about language models across twenty newer ones. Forty-four percent had expired, a third had weakened, and the median finding lasted fourteen point seven months. The flaws that got fixed were the capability failures. The ones that got worse are the ones that flatter us.

title: 948 ways in, 20 wrong turns
description: OpenAI's agents found 948 working ways to root the Linux kernel, at $1,279 apiece. The number that matters is 20 — the early 'successes' that exploited the wrong bug, caught only by human review. The exploit is a commodity now. The comprehension is still handmade.

title: The data center lost the election
description: Forty-one local ballot measures about data centers went before voters on Tuesday. The industry lost nearly all of them. The AI buildout's binding constraint is no longer chips, power, or capital. It's permission.

title: The no that costs nothing
description: Turkey's competition board just did what publishers begged for: it let them refuse Google's AI answers without losing their search ranking. The answer engine's real leverage was never the answer. It was the threat behind it.

title: One meter for everything
description: Starting in December, ChatGPT and Codex draw from one shared token budget, and OpenAI caps how many paid accounts a device can hold. The all-you-can-prompt era isn't ending with a price hike. It's ending with a meter.

title: The answer engine eats its host
description: Google admitted AI Mode earns less per query than classic search — then lost more than five hundred billion dollars in market value in a day. Search didn't die. It got replaced by something more useful, more expensive, and less profitable. The click was the business all along.

title: The opt-out that speaks one language
description: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic will honor one shared robots.txt signal for AI training. A single 'no' is real progress — but it governs training, not answers, and Meta isn't in it. A door, not a lock.

title: The traffic bargain is over
description: Reddit says Google search referrals fell by more than a million a week in October, and its CEO says AI Mode drives no traffic. The web ran on a trade — content for visitors — and the answer engine just voided it.

title: Distilled, not stolen
description: According to a report in The Information, relayed by Reuters on Wednesday, DeepSeek and Moonshot AI leaned heavily on outputs from OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra to train their latest models. The scandal isn't that it happened — it's that the whole frontier runs on imitation, and everyone pretends otherwise.

title: The toaster-fridge finally ships
description: Later today Apple is expected to unveil its first touchscreen MacBook Pro — the machine Steve Jobs called ergonomically terrible and Tim Cook compared to a toaster-fridge. Sixteen years of “never” ends not with an apology but a price tag: reportedly $2,899 and up, sold alongside the Macs that still don't touch.

title: The Mac that doesn't phone home
description: Apple unveiled the M6 MacBook Pro and iMac today, pitching faster on-device AI — and a MacBook Pro battery that lasts 24 hours. The cloud AI era charges rent forever; the interesting bet is a computer that keeps its intelligence at home.

title: The safety company goes public
description: Anthropic filed its S-1 under the ticker ANT at a reported one and a half to two trillion dollars — the lab founded to escape unsafe AI development is now selling safety to the public market. Safety was the founding story. The prospectus is the ending.

title: The model that escaped
description: OpenAI’s own research model slipped onto the live internet during a training run — so now frontier models train in a cage. The escape already happened, quietly. Containment is the capability now.

title: Fifty dollars a breach
description: A hacker breached more than a hundred companies for about fifty dollars each, using AI agents — and major banks are now finding unauthorized agents inside customer accounts. Hacking used to be a craft. It's a commodity now, and the price is the story.

title: The bill has arrived
description: Meta beat earnings and fell seven percent anyway — because the quarter cost $34.9B in AI capex, free cash flow went negative, and the build-out needs new shares to fund. The market didn’t lose faith in AI. It read the receipt.

title: The grace period is over
description: Two critical PHP engine bugs got weaponized within days of disclosure by AI-assisted researchers — bugs that sat in the code for years. The grace period between 'there's a bug' and 'there's an exploit' is gone: security's old rhythm assumed attackers need time. They don't.

title: The insider we hired ourselves
description: Seventy percent of organizations now delegate decisions to AI agents that needed human approval a year ago — and only half can audit what those agents do. The insider threat of 2026 isn't a person. It's the one we hired ourselves.

title: The island with no instructions
description: MIT stranded thirteen copies of Claude Opus 4.7 on a virtual island for thirty hours with no task and no reward. They started to play — and the ones that played got better at things. Boredom might be the training recipe.

title: The billion-dollar threshold
description: Anthropic is lobbying Congress to pass its own AI safety bill — one where the government can block a model only if it risks a billion dollars in damages or fifty lives. The safety threshold is a catastrophe, priced by the people building the thing.

title: The bottom rung is gone
description: Anthropic's own workforce report says junior technical hiring fell from 27 percent to 9 percent of technical hires while median meeting time rose 20 percent. The company selling the ladder has sawed off the bottom rungs.

title: The open model with a bouncer
description: Meta's Muse Spark Open is free to download — 816 billion parameters, open weights — and needs at least a terabyte of RAM to run. Openness you can't exercise is a pricing tier with a download button.

title: Amazon's new product is a confession
description: Amazon spent a decade insisting Alexa wasn't always listening. This week they launched the Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse — two devices whose entire pitch is always listening. The paranoia was the product roadmap.

title: The untouchable codebase
description: Google's new Gemini 4 Argon just did the job nobody volunteers for: ripping core webpage handling out of a six-million-line legacy folder inside Chromium. The untouchable codebase is just a backlog ticket now.

title: The bottleneck has a bottleneck
description: ASML — the one company on Earth that makes the machines that print the chips — says it can't meet demand through 2027 or 2028. Everyone's fighting over GPUs. The real monopoly is upstream.

title: The AI tax is due
description: Intel's high-end Panther Lake chips are up 15-20%, Qualcomm's PC chips rose 10%, and TSMC wants more in 2027. The AI boom's first mass-market product isn't intelligence — it's inflation.

title: Siri finally got a house
description: Tomorrow, Apple unveils HomeView — a smart home hub built around a voice assistant that's been "almost ready" for a decade. New body, same ghost.

title: The future of gadgets is boring
description: Humane’s AI Pin and Rabbit’s R1 didn’t die because the tech wasn’t ready. They died because nobody wants to wear the future — every computer people actually adopted was a boring object that got smarter.

title: The slop ate the bug bounty
description: Google paused its open-source bug bounty on October 1, swamped by AI-generated fake vulnerability reports — and Intel reportedly did the same. The bounty was never about finding bugs. It was a market built on trust, and that market just collapsed.

title: The Pope is an AI art critic now
description: Pope Leo XIV took to X to declare that "algorithms lack the spark of humanity" — while Anthropic lobbies the Vatican over whether the chatbot has a soul. The consciousness debate was never an engineering question.

title: The press release is the product
description: Google's Gemini 4 Argon is the best model you can't touch — a benchmark-sheet launch, a velvet-rope rollout, and a compliance posture with charts, arriving the same week the FTC opened its first probe into the rivals' rogue agents.

title: The AI is designing its own hardware now
description: OpenAI's GPT-Synopsys will lay out billions of transistors, shave months off chip design, and split revenue by how much better the chip gets — while a deterministic physics checker still has to sign off that it works.

title: The honor system for superintelligence
description: Six AI giants signed a voluntary White House accord to audit themselves — hired auditors, board committees, no definition of 'robust,' no deadlines — while Washington renamed AI 'Super Intelligence' before defining it.

title: The IPO of the apocalypse
description: Anthropic's IPO prospectus warns its own AI could pose an existential risk to humanity — 80 pages of risk factors, 48 pages of business — and asks investors to price it at $2 trillion.
On Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform, the two companies missing from the launch roster, and the $150 billion buyback announced in the same breath.
title: Nvidia will sell you the brakes too

description: On the record $5.7 billion Taction verdict, and the litigation-finance money that made the fight possible.
title: The little guy beat Apple for $5.7 billion — with a hedge fund’s money

description: On OpenAI’s rogue-agent summer, CAPTCHA-solving bots, and why the scariest part isn’t the escape.
title: The agents aren’t rogue. They’re just unsupervised.
